_by: Claude (Anthropic), written during the build on 2026-11-07 from the data shown in Threads. Verify against published editions before relying on it.

Deut.32.8.title: Deuteronomy 32:8: sons of Israel or sons of God?
body: The Masoretic Text ends the verse 'according to the number of the sons of Israel' (בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל).

4QDeut-j (4Q37), fragment 12, line 14, has the letters בני אלוהים, 'sons of God'. In Abegg's transcription both words are preserved letters, while the start of the verse on lines 13 and 14 is the editor's reconstruction.
The Septuagint (Swete) reads 'according to the number of the angels of God' (ἀγγέλων θεοῦ), which points to a Hebrew text like the scroll's.
The BSB follows the scroll here ('the sons of God'). The KJV and WEB follow the Masoretic Text.

Why it matters: the reading ties the nations to the heavenly 'sons of God' (compare Deut 4:19; Ps 82; Dan 10:13, 20). That is a real textual question, so a claim resting on either reading of this verse has a variant dependency.
Deut.32.8.editions: Published in Discoveries in the Judaean Desert XIV (1995).

1Sam.10.27.title: 1 Samuel 10:27 to 11:1: the missing Nahash paragraph
body: 4QSam-a (4Q51), fragment 10a, lines 6 to 9, has a passage the Masoretic Text lacks, placed between 10:27 and 11:1. The lines are shown word by word below from Abegg's transcription.

It tells of Nahash king of the Ammonites oppressing the Gadites and the Reubenites by force and gouging out every right eye, of Israelites beyond the Jordan, and of 'seven thousand men'. Line 9 then reads 'and it happened about a month later' (ויהי כמו חדש) before Nahash goes up against Jabesh.

Several words in this stretch are the editor's reconstruction (shown faded). Read the order of the last line with care: in this transcription the words about reaching Jabesh-gilead follow 'encamped against Jabesh'.
Josephus tells the same story (Antiquities 6.68 to 71 in the standard numbering; 6.5.1 in Whiston's), so a text with this paragraph was known in the first century.
The BSB, KJV and WEB do not include it. Some modern translations (for example the NRSV) do.
1Sam.10.27.editions: Published in Discoveries in the Judaean Desert XVII (2005).

Ps.145.13.title: Psalm 145:13: the missing nun line
body: Psalm 145 is an alphabetic acrostic, but in the Masoretic Text the line for the letter nun is missing: verse 13 (mem) is followed by verse 14 (samek).

11QPs-a (11Q5), column 17, has the line נאמן אלוהים בדבריו וחסיד בכול מעשיו, 'God is faithful in his words and kind in all his works'. The scroll also repeats the refrain 'Blessed be the LORD and blessed be his name for ever and ever' after each line.
Brenton's English of the Septuagint includes the line ('The Lord is faithful in his words, and holy in all his works'). In the Swete Greek given in Threads for this verse the line does not appear.
STEPBible's Hebrew includes the line as 'X' words: Hebrew reconstructed from the Septuagint in the apparatus of BHS. Threads shows those words, marked, but never counts them as Masoretic.
The BSB and the WEB include the line (BSB: 'The LORD is faithful in all His words and kind in all His actions'). The KJV does not.
Ps.145.13.editions: Published in Discoveries in the Judaean Desert IV (1965).

Isa.53.11.title: Isaiah 53:11: 'he will see light'
body: The Masoretic Text reads 'from the anguish of his soul he will see; he will be satisfied', with no object for 'see'.
The Great Isaiah Scroll (1QIsa-a), 1QIsa-b (1Q8) and 4QIsa-d (4Q58) all add אור, 'light': 'he will see light'. In each the word is preserved, not reconstructed.
The Septuagint has 'to show him light' (δεῖξαι αὐτῷ φῶς).

1QIsa-a also reads עבדו, 'his servant', where the Masoretic Text has עבדי, 'my servant', and adds 'and' before two words (וישבע, ובדעתו). Those are separate differences; the other scrolls here agree with the Masoretic 'my servant'.
The BSB ('He will see the light of life') and the WEB ('he will see the light') follow the scrolls. The KJV follows the Masoretic Text.
Isa.53.11.editions: 1QIsa-a and 1QIsa-b: Discoveries in the Judaean Desert XXXII (2010). 4QIsa-d: Discoveries in the Judaean Desert XV (1997).

Jer.10.5.title: Jeremiah 10: the shorter Jeremiah of 4QJer-b
body: The Septuagint of Jeremiah is about one-seventh shorter than the Masoretic Text and arranges some material differently.

4QJer-b (4Q71), fragment 1, covers Jeremiah 9:22 to 10:21. Reading its lines in order, the verse labels run 10:4, 10:9, 10:5, 10:11: there is no 10:6, 10:7, 10:8 or 10:10, and verse 9 stands before verse 5. That is the shape of the Septuagint at this point, not the Masoretic one.

Caution: much of this fragment is the editor's reconstruction (faded in Threads), and the reconstruction itself follows the Septuagint's order. The preserved letters support the shorter form, but the case rests on few words.
The verses missing from 4Q71 (10:6 to 8 and 10:10) are praises of the LORD's greatness set against the idols. A claim built on those verses has a variant dependency.
Jer.10.5.editions: Published in Discoveries in the Judaean Desert XV (1997).

link_reasons.Num.11.29|Joel.2.28: Moses wishes that all the LORD's people were prophets with his Spirit on them; Joel promises the Spirit poured on all flesh so that sons and daughters prophesy.
link_reasons.Num.11.25|Num.11.29: The Spirit rests on the seventy elders and they prophesy, which leads to Moses' wish.
link_reasons.Joel.2.28|Acts.2.17: Peter quotes this promise to explain Pentecost. Where the Septuagint has 'after these things', Peter says 'in the last days'.
link_reasons.Joel.2.29|Acts.2.18: Peter's 'my servants and my handmaids' follows the Septuagint wording; he adds 'and they will prophesy'.
link_reasons.Joel.2.30|Acts.2.19: Peter adds 'above' and 'below' and 'signs' to the Septuagint's 'wonders in heaven and on the earth'.
link_reasons.Joel.2.31|Acts.2.20: Peter keeps the Septuagint's 'great and glorious day' where the Hebrew has 'great and terrible'.
link_reasons.Joel.2.32|Acts.2.21: Peter stops the quotation at 'everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved'.
link_reasons.Joel.2.32|Rom.10.13: Paul quotes the same line of Joel about calling on the name of the Lord.
link_reasons.Acts.2.17|Isa.2.2: Peter's phrase 'in the last days' matches the Septuagint wording of Isaiah 2:2.
link_reasons.Ezek.36.27|Ezek.37.14: 'I will put my Spirit within you' returns at the end of the dry bones vision.
link_reasons.Ezek.36.27|Joel.2.28: Both promise God's own Spirit given to his people in the restoration.
link_reasons.Ezek.39.29|Joel.2.28: Both speak of God pouring out his Spirit on his people.
link_reasons.Ezek.36.26|Ezek.11.19: Ezekiel gives the promise of a new heart and a new spirit twice.
link_reasons.Luke.24.49|Acts.1.4: The 'promise of my Father' is named again just before the Ascension.
link_reasons.Luke.24.49|Acts.1.8: 'Power from on high' is explained as power when the Holy Spirit comes upon you.
link_reasons.Luke.24.49|Acts.2.33: Peter says the exalted Jesus received the promised Spirit from the Father and poured it out.
link_reasons.Acts.2.4|Acts.10.46: Speaking in tongues marks the Spirit's coming on Gentiles as it did at Pentecost.
link_reasons.Acts.2.4|Acts.19.6: The Spirit comes on the Ephesian disciples and they speak in tongues and prophesy.
link_reasons.Acts.2.38|Acts.2.39: The gift of the Holy Spirit is promised to 'you and your children and all who are far off'.

journey_notes.spirit.joel: Hebrew and Septuagint compared. In 2:28 (Hebrew 3:1) the Hebrew has 'I will pour out my Spirit' (אֶת־רוּחִי); the Septuagint has 'I will pour out from my Spirit' (ἀπὸ τοῦ πνεύματός μου), which Brenton renders 'of my Spirit'. In 2:29 the Hebrew has 'on the male servants and the female servants'; the Septuagint has 'on my male servants and on the female servants', which Peter takes up in Acts 2:18, adding 'my' to both. In 2:31 the Hebrew calls the day 'great and terrible'; the Septuagint has 'great and glorious' (ἐπιφανῆ), as Acts 2:20 does. At the end of 2:32 the Hebrew has 'among the survivors whom the LORD calls'; the Septuagint has 'and those who have good news announced to them, whom the Lord has called'.
journey_notes.spirit.acts: The table above is computed, not written: it lines up the Greek of Acts 2:17 to 21 (SBLGNT) with the Septuagint of Joel 2:28 to 32 (Swete) word by word. Words only in Acts are marked; words only in the Septuagint are marked. Read the differences as Peter's (or Luke's) shaping of the quotation for the moment, not as a different text of Joel.
journey_notes.spirit.1qs: The Community Rule speaks of a holy spirit that cleanses (3:7; 4:21), of the prophets revealing by God's holy spirit (8:16), and of the community itself as a foundation of a holy spirit (9:3). This is Tier 3: background to the New Testament world, not Scripture. It can illuminate how 'holy spirit' language was used, but it carries no authority.
